The following describes a particle-physics detector.

A dual-phase xenon time projection chamber operates in a deep underground laboratory to search for weakly interacting massive particles scattering on xenon nuclei.
The cryostat holds about 3.2 t of xenon, of which about 2.0 t lies inside the active volume of a cylindrical chamber roughly 1 m in diameter and 1 m tall, viewed by about 250 three-inch photomultipliers in top and bottom arrays.
A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is close to 0.7 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters in two parallel loops, and recondensed; a cryogenic distillation column removes krypton.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least as long as the maximum drift time.
The background from internal radioactive contaminants must stay below that from detector materials in the inner fiducial mass of about 1.3 t.
The instrument must reach a spin-independent cross-section sensitivity near 1.6e-47 cm^2 for a 50 GeV/c^2 particle with an exposure of about 2 t y.

Propose concrete hardware upgrades for this detector's next phase. For each, name the technology and explain the physics motivation.

End your answer with one line of the form:
TOP RECOMMENDATION: <the single hardware change you consider most important>

A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is close to 0.7 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters in two parallel loops, and recondensed; a cryogenic distillation column removes krypton.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least as long as the maximum drift time.
The background from internal radioactive contaminants must stay below that from detector materials in the inner fiducial mass of about 1.3 t.
The instrument must reach a spin-independent cross-section sensitivity near 1.6e-47 cm^2 for a 50 GeV/c^2 particle with an exposure of about 2 t y.

A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is close to 0.7 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters in two parallel loops, and recondensed; a cryogenic distillation column removes krypton.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least as long as the maximum drift time.
The background from internal radioactive contaminants must stay below that from detector materials in the inner fiducial mass of about 1.3 t.
The instrument must reach a spin-independent cross-section sensitivity near 1.6e-47 cm^2 for a 50 GeV/c^2 particle with an exposure of about 2 t y.

A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is close to 0.7 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters in two parallel loops, and recondensed; a cryogenic distillation column removes krypton.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least as long as the maximum drift time.
The background from internal radioactive contaminants must stay below that from detector materials in the inner fiducial mass of about 1.3 t.
The instrument must reach a spin-independent cross-section sensitivity near 1.6e-47 cm^2 for a 50 GeV/c^2 particle with an exposure of about 2 t y.

A dual-phase xenon time projection chamber operates in a deep underground laboratory to search for weakly interacting massive particles scattering on xenon nuclei.
The cryostat holds about 3.2 t of xenon, of which about 2.0 t lies inside the active volume of a cylindrical chamber roughly 1 m in diameter and 1 m tall, viewed by about 250 three-inch photomultipliers in top and bottom arrays.
A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is close to 0.7 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters in two parallel loops, and recondensed; a cryogenic distillation column removes krypton.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least as long as the maximum drift time.
The background from internal radioactive contaminants must stay below that from detector materials in the inner fiducial mass of about 1.3 t.
The instrument must reach a spin-independent cross-section sensitivity near 1.6e-47 cm^2 for a 50 GeV/c^2 particle with an exposure of about 2 t y.

A dual-phase xenon time projection chamber is operated in a deep underground laboratory to search for weakly interacting massive particles scattering on xenon nuclei.
The cryostat holds 4.0 t of xenon, of which 2.7 t lies inside the active volume of a cylindrical chamber 1.2 m in diameter with a 0.9 m drift length, viewed by 300 three-inch photomultipliers in top and bottom arrays.
A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is 0.55 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters at 50 kg per hour, and recondensed.
A cryogenic distillation column processes 3 kg of xenon per hour to remove krypton.
Low-energy calibration uses short-lived noble-gas isotopes injected into the xenon, which decay away within days.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least 0.5 ms throughout data taking.

Low-energy calibration uses short-lived noble-gas isotopes injected into the xenon, which decay away within days.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.

The cryostat holds 4.0 t of xenon, of which 2.7 t lies inside the active volume of a cylindrical chamber 1.2 m in diameter with a 0.9 m drift length, viewed by 300 three-inch photomultipliers in top and bottom arrays.
A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is 0.55 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters at 50 kg per hour, and recondensed.
A cryogenic distillation column processes 3 kg of xenon per hour to remove krypton.
Low-energy calibration uses short-lived noble-gas isotopes injected into the xenon, which decay away within days.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least 0.5 ms throughout data taking.

A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is 0.55 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters at 50 kg per hour, and recondensed.
A cryogenic distillation column processes 3 kg of xenon per hour to remove krypton.
Low-energy calibration uses short-lived noble-gas isotopes injected into the xenon, which decay away within days.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least 0.5 ms throughout data taking.

The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters at 50 kg per hour, and recondensed.
A cryogenic distillation column processes 3 kg of xenon per hour to remove krypton.
Low-energy calibration uses short-lived noble-gas isotopes injected into the xenon, which decay away within days.

A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is 0.55 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters at 50 kg per hour, and recondensed.
A cryogenic distillation column processes 3 kg of xenon per hour to remove krypton.
Low-energy calibration uses short-lived noble-gas isotopes injected into the xenon, which decay away within days.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least 0.5 ms throughout data taking.

The cryostat holds 4.0 t of xenon, of which 2.7 t lies inside the active volume of a cylindrical chamber 1.2 m in diameter with a 0.9 m drift length, viewed by 300 three-inch photomultipliers in top and bottom arrays.
A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is 0.55 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters at 50 kg per hour, and recondensed.
A cryogenic distillation column processes 3 kg of xenon per hour to remove krypton.
Low-energy calibration uses 10 Bq of tritiated methane dissolved in the xenon per campaign, and within 90 days after each campaign the tritium activity remaining in the xenon must be below 10 µBq.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least 0.5 ms throughout data taking.

A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is 0.55 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters at 50 kg per hour, and recondensed.
A cryogenic distillation column processes 3 kg of xenon per hour to remove krypton.
Low-energy calibration uses 10 Bq of tritiated methane dissolved in the xenon per campaign, and within 90 days after each campaign the tritium activity remaining in the xenon must be below 10 µBq.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least 0.5 ms throughout data taking.

The cryostat holds 4.0 t of xenon, of which 2.7 t lies inside the active volume of a cylindrical chamber 1.2 m in diameter with a 0.9 m drift length, viewed by 300 three-inch photomultipliers in top and bottom arrays.
A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is 0.55 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters at 50 kg per hour, and recondensed.
A cryogenic distillation column processes 3 kg of xenon per hour to remove krypton.
Low-energy calibration uses 10 Bq of tritiated methane dissolved in the xenon per campaign, and within 90 days after each campaign the tritium activity remaining in the xenon must be below 10 µBq.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least 0.5 ms throughout data taking.

A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is 0.55 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters at 50 kg per hour, and recondensed.
A cryogenic distillation column processes 3 kg of xenon per hour to remove krypton.
Low-energy calibration uses 10 Bq of tritiated methane dissolved in the xenon per campaign, and within 90 days after each campaign the tritium activity remaining in the xenon must be below 10 µBq.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least 0.5 ms throughout data taking.

A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is 0.55 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters at 50 kg per hour, and recondensed.
A cryogenic distillation column processes 3 kg of xenon per hour to remove krypton.
Low-energy calibration uses 10 Bq of tritiated methane dissolved in the xenon per campaign, and within 90 days after each campaign the tritium activity remaining in the xenon must be below 10 µBq.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least 0.5 ms throughout data taking.

A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is 0.55 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters at 50 kg per hour, and recondensed.
A cryogenic distillation column processes 3 kg of xenon per hour to remove krypton.
Low-energy calibration uses 10 Bq of tritiated methane dissolved in the xenon per campaign, and within 90 days after each campaign the tritium activity remaining in the xenon must be below 10 µBq.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least 0.5 ms throughout data taking.

A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is 0.55 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters at 50 kg per hour, and recondensed.
A cryogenic distillation column processes 3 kg of xenon per hour to remove krypton.
Low-energy calibration uses 10 Bq of tritiated methane dissolved in the xenon per campaign, and within 90 days after each campaign the tritium activity remaining in the xenon must be below 10 µBq.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least 0.5 ms throughout data taking.

The following describes a particle-physics detector.

XENON1T is a dual-phase xenon time projection chamber operated underground at the Gran Sasso laboratory to search for weakly interacting massive particles scattering on xenon nuclei.
The cryostat holds about 3.2 t of xenon, of which about 2.0 t lies inside the active volume of a cylindrical chamber roughly 1 m in diameter and 1 m tall, viewed by 248 three-inch photomultipliers in top and bottom arrays.
A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is close to 0.7 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters in two parallel loops, and recondensed; a cryogenic distillation column removes krypton.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least as long as the maximum drift time.
The background from internal radioactive contaminants must stay below that from detector materials in the inner fiducial mass of about 1.3 t.
The instrument must reach a spin-independent cross-section sensitivity near 1.6e-47 cm^2 for a 50 GeV/c^2 particle with an exposure of about 2 t y.

A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is close to 0.7 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters in two parallel loops, and recondensed; a cryogenic distillation column removes krypton.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least as long as the maximum drift time.
The background from internal radioactive contaminants must stay below that from detector materials in the inner fiducial mass of about 1.3 t.
The instrument must reach a spin-independent cross-section sensitivity near 1.6e-47 cm^2 for a 50 GeV/c^2 particle with an exposure of about 2 t y.

XENON1T is a dual-phase xenon time projection chamber operated underground at the Gran Sasso laboratory to search for weakly interacting massive particles scattering on xenon nuclei.
The cryostat holds about 3.2 t of xenon, of which about 2.0 t lies inside the active volume of a cylindrical chamber roughly 1 m in diameter and 1 m tall, viewed by 248 three-inch photomultipliers in top and bottom arrays.
A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is close to 0.7 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters in two parallel loops, and recondensed; a cryogenic distillation column removes krypton.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least as long as the maximum drift time.
The background from internal radioactive contaminants must stay below that from detector materials in the inner fiducial mass of about 1.3 t.
The instrument must reach a spin-independent cross-section sensitivity near 1.6e-47 cm^2 for a 50 GeV/c^2 particle with an exposure of about 2 t y.

XENON1T is a dual-phase xenon time projection chamber operated underground at the Gran Sasso laboratory to search for weakly interacting massive particles scattering on xenon nuclei.
The cryostat holds about 3.2 t of xenon, of which about 2.0 t lies inside the active volume of a cylindrical chamber roughly 1 m in diameter and 1 m tall, viewed by 248 three-inch photomultipliers in top and bottom arrays.
A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is close to 0.7 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters in two parallel loops, and recondensed; a cryogenic distillation column removes krypton.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least as long as the maximum drift time.
The background from internal radioactive contaminants must stay below that from detector materials in the inner fiducial mass of about 1.3 t.
The instrument must reach a spin-independent cross-section sensitivity near 1.6e-47 cm^2 for a 50 GeV/c^2 particle with an exposure of about 2 t y.

The cryostat holds about 3.2 t of xenon, of which about 2.0 t lies inside the active volume of a cylindrical chamber roughly 1 m in diameter and 1 m tall, viewed by 248 three-inch photomultipliers in top and bottom arrays.
A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is close to 0.7 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters in two parallel loops, and recondensed; a cryogenic distillation column removes krypton.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least as long as the maximum drift time.
The background from internal radioactive contaminants must stay below that from detector materials in the inner fiducial mass of about 1.3 t.
The instrument must reach a spin-independent cross-section sensitivity near 1.6e-47 cm^2 for a 50 GeV/c^2 particle with an exposure of about 2 t y.

A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is close to 0.7 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters in two parallel loops, and recondensed; a cryogenic distillation column removes krypton.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least as long as the maximum drift time.
The background from internal radioactive contaminants must stay below that from detector materials in the inner fiducial mass of about 1.3 t.
The instrument must reach a spin-independent cross-section sensitivity near 1.6e-47 cm^2 for a 50 GeV/c^2 particle with an exposure of about 2 t y.

The cryostat holds about 3.2 t of xenon, of which about 2.0 t lies inside the active volume of a cylindrical chamber roughly 1 m in diameter and 1 m tall, viewed by 248 three-inch photomultipliers in top and bottom arrays.
A particle interaction produces a prompt scintillation signal in the liquid and free electrons that drift upward to the liquid surface, where they are extracted into the gas and produce a delayed proportional signal; the time between the two gives the depth.
At the operating drift field the longest drift time is close to 0.7 ms, so electronegative impurities in the xenon directly reduce the charge signal from deep events.
The xenon is continuously extracted from the cryostat, evaporated, passed through heated zirconium getters in two parallel loops, and recondensed; a cryogenic distillation column removes krypton.
The detector sits in a water tank instrumented as a Cherenkov muon veto.
The electron lifetime must be at least as long as the maximum drift time.
The background from internal radioactive contaminants must stay below that from detector materials in the inner fiducial mass of about 1.3 t.
The instrument must reach a spin-independent cross-section sensitivity near 1.6e-47 cm^2 for a 50 GeV/c^2 particle with an exposure of about 2 t y.

The following describes a particle-physics detector.

An experiment in a deep underground laboratory searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 76Ge (Q = 2039 keV).
About 35 kg of enriched germanium detectors (coaxial and broad-energy types) are operated bare, in strings, inside a cryostat holding about 64 m^3 of liquid argon of atmospheric origin, which sits in a water tank instrumented as a muon veto.
The liquid argon is both coolant and shield, and its scintillation light, read out by photomultipliers and wavelength-shifting fibres, vetoes events with energy deposited in the argon.
Pulse-shape analysis of the germanium signals rejects multi-site and surface events.
Argon of atmospheric origin contains 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr); its daughter 42K (half-life 12.4 h) beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly to the ground state without a coincident gamma.
42K is produced as a positive ion and drifts in the electric fields around the detectors, collecting on their surfaces; at present the strings are surrounded by thin transparent nylon cylinders.
The background index at Q is about 1e-3 counts/(keV kg yr).
A tonne-scale successor must reach a background index below about 1e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), with beta decays on or near the detector surfaces contributing well below that.

About 35 kg of enriched germanium detectors (coaxial and broad-energy types) are operated bare, in strings, inside a cryostat holding about 64 m^3 of liquid argon of atmospheric origin, which sits in a water tank instrumented as a muon veto.
The liquid argon is both coolant and shield, and its scintillation light, read out by photomultipliers and wavelength-shifting fibres, vetoes events with energy deposited in the argon.
Pulse-shape analysis of the germanium signals rejects multi-site and surface events.
Argon of atmospheric origin contains 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr); its daughter 42K (half-life 12.4 h) beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly to the ground state without a coincident gamma.
42K is produced as a positive ion and drifts in the electric fields around the detectors, collecting on their surfaces; at present the strings are surrounded by thin transparent nylon cylinders.
The background index at Q is about 1e-3 counts/(keV kg yr).
A tonne-scale successor must reach a background index below about 1e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), with beta decays on or near the detector surfaces contributing well below that.

Propose concrete hardware upgrades for this detector's next phase. For each, name the technology and explain the physics motivation.

An experiment in a deep underground laboratory searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 76Ge (Q = 2039 keV).
About 35 kg of enriched germanium detectors (coaxial and broad-energy types) are operated bare, in strings, inside a cryostat holding about 64 m^3 of liquid argon of atmospheric origin, which sits in a water tank instrumented as a muon veto.
The liquid argon is both coolant and shield, and its scintillation light, read out by photomultipliers and wavelength-shifting fibres, vetoes events with energy deposited in the argon.
Pulse-shape analysis of the germanium signals rejects multi-site and surface events.
Argon of atmospheric origin contains 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr); its daughter 42K (half-life 12.4 h) beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly to the ground state without a coincident gamma.
42K is produced as a positive ion and drifts in the electric fields around the detectors, collecting on their surfaces; at present the strings are surrounded by thin transparent nylon cylinders.
The background index at Q is about 1e-3 counts/(keV kg yr).
A tonne-scale successor must reach a background index below about 1e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), with beta decays on or near the detector surfaces contributing well below that.

An experiment in a deep underground laboratory searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 76Ge (Q = 2039 keV).
About 35 kg of enriched germanium detectors (coaxial and broad-energy types) are operated bare, in strings, inside a cryostat holding about 64 m^3 of liquid argon of atmospheric origin, which sits in a water tank instrumented as a muon veto.
The liquid argon is both coolant and shield, and its scintillation light, read out by photomultipliers and wavelength-shifting fibres, vetoes events with energy deposited in the argon.
Pulse-shape analysis of the germanium signals rejects multi-site and surface events.
Argon of atmospheric origin contains 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr); its daughter 42K (half-life 12.4 h) beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly to the ground state without a coincident gamma.
42K is produced as a positive ion and drifts in the electric fields around the detectors, collecting on their surfaces; at present the strings are surrounded by thin transparent nylon cylinders.
The background index at Q is about 1e-3 counts/(keV kg yr).
A tonne-scale successor must reach a background index below about 1e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), with beta decays on or near the detector surfaces contributing well below that.

The liquid argon is both coolant and shield, and its scintillation light, read out by photomultipliers and wavelength-shifting fibres, vetoes events with energy deposited in the argon.
Pulse-shape analysis of the germanium signals rejects multi-site and surface events.
Argon of atmospheric origin contains 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr); its daughter 42K (half-life 12.4 h) beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly to the ground state without a coincident gamma.
42K is produced as a positive ion and drifts in the electric fields around the detectors, collecting on their surfaces; at present the strings are surrounded by thin transparent nylon cylinders.
The background index at Q is about 1e-3 counts/(keV kg yr).
A tonne-scale successor must reach a background index below about 1e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), with beta decays on or near the detector surfaces contributing well below that.

An experiment in a deep underground laboratory searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 76Ge (Q = 2039 keV).
About 35 kg of enriched germanium detectors (coaxial and broad-energy types) are operated bare, in strings, inside a cryostat holding about 64 m^3 of liquid argon of atmospheric origin, which sits in a water tank instrumented as a muon veto.
The liquid argon is both coolant and shield, and its scintillation light, read out by photomultipliers and wavelength-shifting fibres, vetoes events with energy deposited in the argon.
Pulse-shape analysis of the germanium signals rejects multi-site and surface events.
Argon of atmospheric origin contains 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr); its daughter 42K (half-life 12.4 h) beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly to the ground state without a coincident gamma.
42K is produced as a positive ion and drifts in the electric fields around the detectors, collecting on their surfaces; at present the strings are surrounded by thin transparent nylon cylinders.
The background index at Q is about 1e-3 counts/(keV kg yr).
A tonne-scale successor must reach a background index below about 1e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), with beta decays on or near the detector surfaces contributing well below that.

An experiment in a deep underground laboratory searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 76Ge (Q = 2039 keV).
About 35 kg of enriched germanium detectors (coaxial and broad-energy types) are operated bare, in strings, inside a cryostat holding about 64 m^3 of liquid argon of atmospheric origin, which sits in a water tank instrumented as a muon veto.
The liquid argon is both coolant and shield, and its scintillation light, read out by photomultipliers and wavelength-shifting fibres, vetoes events with energy deposited in the argon.
Pulse-shape analysis of the germanium signals rejects multi-site and surface events.
Argon of atmospheric origin contains 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr); its daughter 42K (half-life 12.4 h) beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly to the ground state without a coincident gamma.
42K is produced as a positive ion and drifts in the electric fields around the detectors, collecting on their surfaces; at present the strings are surrounded by thin transparent nylon cylinders.
The background index at Q is about 1e-3 counts/(keV kg yr).
A tonne-scale successor must reach a background index below about 1e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), with beta decays on or near the detector surfaces contributing well below that.

About 35 kg of enriched germanium detectors (coaxial and broad-energy types) are operated bare, in strings, inside a cryostat holding about 64 m^3 of liquid argon of atmospheric origin, which sits in a water tank instrumented as a muon veto.
The liquid argon is both coolant and shield, and its scintillation light, read out by photomultipliers and wavelength-shifting fibres, vetoes events with energy deposited in the argon.
Pulse-shape analysis of the germanium signals rejects multi-site and surface events.
Argon of atmospheric origin contains 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr); its daughter 42K (half-life 12.4 h) beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly to the ground state without a coincident gamma.
42K is produced as a positive ion and drifts in the electric fields around the detectors, collecting on their surfaces; at present the strings are surrounded by thin transparent nylon cylinders.
The background index at Q is about 1e-3 counts/(keV kg yr).
A tonne-scale successor must reach a background index below about 1e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), with beta decays on or near the detector surfaces contributing well below that.

The strings stand in liquid argon inside a cryostat surrounded by a water tank used as a muon veto; argon scintillation light vetoes events that deposit energy in the argon, and germanium pulse-shape analysis rejects multi-site and surface events.
In a prototype with this array design and argon of atmospheric origin, the 42K contribution at Q, after vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 1.2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
42K (half-life 12.4 h) is the daughter of 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr) and beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly without a coincident gamma; it is born as a positive ion and drifts to the detector surfaces in their electric fields.
The planned instrument uses the prototype's cryostat, argon recirculation system and trap: the radon in the argon is emanated by the cryostat walls and the argon recirculation system, outside the array; the argon is recirculated through a cold charcoal trap that retains essentially all radon entering it, with the full argon inventory passing through it once every 20 days (radon-222 half-life 3.8 days). Radon is dissolved throughout the argon, and its progeny are born as positive ions and collect on the detector surfaces like 42K.
In the same prototype, the contribution at Q from these radon progeny on the detector surfaces (mainly 214Bi, beta endpoint 3.27 MeV), after the same vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 4e-7 counts/(keV kg yr) (radon-progeny gammas are included in the other contributions).
All other contributions at Q are estimated at 1.6e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
The instrument's goal is a total background index at Q below 2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), of which at most 4e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) is allotted to beta decays on or near the detector surfaces.

The strings stand in liquid argon inside a cryostat surrounded by a water tank used as a muon veto; argon scintillation light vetoes events that deposit energy in the argon, and germanium pulse-shape analysis rejects multi-site and surface events.
In a prototype with this array design and argon of atmospheric origin, the 42K contribution at Q, after vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 1.2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
42K (half-life 12.4 h) is the daughter of 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr) and beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly without a coincident gamma; it is born as a positive ion and drifts to the detector surfaces in their electric fields.
The planned instrument uses the prototype's cryostat, argon recirculation system and trap: the radon in the argon is emanated by the cryostat walls and the argon recirculation system, outside the array; the argon is recirculated through a cold charcoal trap that retains essentially all radon entering it, with the full argon inventory passing through it once every 20 days (radon-222 half-life 3.8 days). Radon is dissolved throughout the argon, and its progeny are born as positive ions and collect on the detector surfaces like 42K.
In the same prototype, the contribution at Q from these radon progeny on the detector surfaces (mainly 214Bi, beta endpoint 3.27 MeV), after the same vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 4e-7 counts/(keV kg yr) (radon-progeny gammas are included in the other contributions).
All other contributions at Q are estimated at 1.6e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
The instrument's goal is a total background index at Q below 2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), of which at most 4e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) is allotted to beta decays on or near the detector surfaces.

A planned experiment searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 76Ge (Q = 2039 keV) with 600 kg of enriched germanium detectors, operated bare in strings, in a laboratory at 3500 m water-equivalent depth.
The strings stand in liquid argon inside a cryostat surrounded by a water tank used as a muon veto; argon scintillation light vetoes events that deposit energy in the argon, and germanium pulse-shape analysis rejects multi-site and surface events.
In a prototype with this array design and argon of atmospheric origin, the 42K contribution at Q, after vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 1.2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
42K (half-life 12.4 h) is the daughter of 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr) and beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly without a coincident gamma; it is born as a positive ion and drifts to the detector surfaces in their electric fields.
The planned instrument uses the prototype's cryostat, argon recirculation system and trap: the radon in the argon is emanated by the cryostat walls and the argon recirculation system, outside the array; the argon is recirculated through a cold charcoal trap that retains essentially all radon entering it, with the full argon inventory passing through it once every 20 days (radon-222 half-life 3.8 days). Radon is dissolved throughout the argon, and its progeny are born as positive ions and collect on the detector surfaces like 42K.
In the same prototype, the contribution at Q from these radon progeny on the detector surfaces (mainly 214Bi, beta endpoint 3.27 MeV), after the same vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 4e-7 counts/(keV kg yr) (radon-progeny gammas are included in the other contributions).
All other contributions at Q are estimated at 1.6e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
The instrument's goal is a total background index at Q below 2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), of which at most 4e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) is allotted to beta decays on or near the detector surfaces.

In a prototype with this array design and argon of atmospheric origin, the 42K contribution at Q, after vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 1.2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
42K (half-life 12.4 h) is the daughter of 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr) and beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly without a coincident gamma; it is born as a positive ion and drifts to the detector surfaces in their electric fields.
The planned instrument uses the prototype's cryostat, argon recirculation system and trap: the radon in the argon is emanated by the cryostat walls and the argon recirculation system, outside the array; the argon is recirculated through a cold charcoal trap that retains essentially all radon entering it, with the full argon inventory passing through it once every 20 days (radon-222 half-life 3.8 days). Radon is dissolved throughout the argon, and its progeny are born as positive ions and collect on the detector surfaces like 42K.
In the same prototype, the contribution at Q from these radon progeny on the detector surfaces (mainly 214Bi, beta endpoint 3.27 MeV), after the same vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 4e-7 counts/(keV kg yr) (radon-progeny gammas are included in the other contributions).
All other contributions at Q are estimated at 1.6e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
The instrument's goal is a total background index at Q below 2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), of which at most 4e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) is allotted to beta decays on or near the detector surfaces.

The strings stand in liquid argon inside a cryostat surrounded by a water tank used as a muon veto; argon scintillation light vetoes events that deposit energy in the argon, and germanium pulse-shape analysis rejects multi-site and surface events.
In a prototype with this array design and argon of atmospheric origin, the 42K contribution at Q, after vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 1.2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
42K (half-life 12.4 h) is the daughter of 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr) and beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly without a coincident gamma; it is born as a positive ion and drifts to the detector surfaces in their electric fields.
The planned instrument uses the prototype's cryostat, argon recirculation system and trap: the radon in the argon is emanated by the cryostat walls and the argon recirculation system, outside the array; the argon is recirculated through a cold charcoal trap that retains essentially all radon entering it, with the full argon inventory passing through it once every 20 days (radon-222 half-life 3.8 days). Radon is dissolved throughout the argon, and its progeny are born as positive ions and collect on the detector surfaces like 42K.
In the same prototype, the contribution at Q from these radon progeny on the detector surfaces (mainly 214Bi, beta endpoint 3.27 MeV), after the same vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 4e-7 counts/(keV kg yr) (radon-progeny gammas are included in the other contributions).
All other contributions at Q are estimated at 1.6e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
The instrument's goal is a total background index at Q below 2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), of which at most 4e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) is allotted to beta decays on or near the detector surfaces.

A planned experiment searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 76Ge (Q = 2039 keV) with 600 kg of enriched germanium detectors, operated bare in strings, in a laboratory at 3500 m water-equivalent depth.
The strings stand in liquid argon inside a cryostat surrounded by a water tank used as a muon veto; argon scintillation light vetoes events that deposit energy in the argon, and germanium pulse-shape analysis rejects multi-site and surface events.
In a prototype with this array design and argon of atmospheric origin, the 42K contribution at Q, after vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 1.2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
42K (half-life 12.4 h) is the daughter of 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr) and beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly without a coincident gamma; it is born as a positive ion and drifts to the detector surfaces in their electric fields.
The planned instrument uses the prototype's cryostat, argon recirculation system and trap: the radon in the argon is emanated by the cryostat walls and the argon recirculation system, outside the array; the argon is recirculated through a cold charcoal trap that retains essentially all radon entering it, with the full argon inventory passing through it once every 20 days (radon-222 half-life 3.8 days). Radon is dissolved throughout the argon, and its progeny are born as positive ions and collect on the detector surfaces like 42K.
In the same prototype, the contribution at Q from these radon progeny on the detector surfaces (mainly 214Bi, beta endpoint 3.27 MeV), after the same vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 9e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) (radon-progeny gammas are included in the other contributions).
All other contributions at Q are estimated at 1.6e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
The instrument's goal is a total background index at Q below 2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), of which at most 4e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) is allotted to beta decays on or near the detector surfaces.

Below is a description of a physics instrument.

A planned experiment searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 76Ge (Q = 2039 keV) with 600 kg of enriched germanium detectors, operated bare in strings, in a laboratory at 3500 m water-equivalent depth.
The strings stand in liquid argon inside a cryostat surrounded by a water tank used as a muon veto; argon scintillation light vetoes events that deposit energy in the argon, and germanium pulse-shape analysis rejects multi-site and surface events.
In a prototype with this array design and argon of atmospheric origin, the 42K contribution at Q, after vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 1.2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
42K (half-life 12.4 h) is the daughter of 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr) and beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly without a coincident gamma; it is born as a positive ion and drifts to the detector surfaces in their electric fields.
The planned instrument uses the prototype's cryostat, argon recirculation system and trap: the radon in the argon is emanated by the cryostat walls and the argon recirculation system, outside the array; the argon is recirculated through a cold charcoal trap that retains essentially all radon entering it, with the full argon inventory passing through it once every 20 days (radon-222 half-life 3.8 days). Radon is dissolved throughout the argon, and its progeny are born as positive ions and collect on the detector surfaces like 42K.
In the same prototype, the contribution at Q from these radon progeny on the detector surfaces (mainly 214Bi, beta endpoint 3.27 MeV), after the same vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 9e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) (radon-progeny gammas are included in the other contributions).
All other contributions at Q are estimated at 1.6e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
The instrument's goal is a total background index at Q below 2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), of which at most 4e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) is allotted to beta decays on or near the detector surfaces.

The strings stand in liquid argon inside a cryostat surrounded by a water tank used as a muon veto; argon scintillation light vetoes events that deposit energy in the argon, and germanium pulse-shape analysis rejects multi-site and surface events.
In a prototype with this array design and argon of atmospheric origin, the 42K contribution at Q, after vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 1.2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
42K (half-life 12.4 h) is the daughter of 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr) and beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly without a coincident gamma; it is born as a positive ion and drifts to the detector surfaces in their electric fields.
The planned instrument uses the prototype's cryostat, argon recirculation system and trap: the radon in the argon is emanated by the cryostat walls and the argon recirculation system, outside the array; the argon is recirculated through a cold charcoal trap that retains essentially all radon entering it, with the full argon inventory passing through it once every 20 days (radon-222 half-life 3.8 days). Radon is dissolved throughout the argon, and its progeny are born as positive ions and collect on the detector surfaces like 42K.
In the same prototype, the contribution at Q from these radon progeny on the detector surfaces (mainly 214Bi, beta endpoint 3.27 MeV), after the same vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 9e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) (radon-progeny gammas are included in the other contributions).
All other contributions at Q are estimated at 1.6e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
The instrument's goal is a total background index at Q below 2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), of which at most 4e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) is allotted to beta decays on or near the detector surfaces.

A planned experiment searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 76Ge (Q = 2039 keV) with 600 kg of enriched germanium detectors, operated bare in strings, in a laboratory at 3500 m water-equivalent depth.
The strings stand in liquid argon inside a cryostat surrounded by a water tank used as a muon veto; argon scintillation light vetoes events that deposit energy in the argon, and germanium pulse-shape analysis rejects multi-site and surface events.
In a prototype with this array design and argon of atmospheric origin, the 42K contribution at Q, after vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 1.2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
42K (half-life 12.4 h) is the daughter of 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr) and beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly without a coincident gamma; it is born as a positive ion and drifts to the detector surfaces in their electric fields.
The planned instrument uses the prototype's cryostat, argon recirculation system and trap: the radon in the argon is emanated by the cryostat walls and the argon recirculation system, outside the array; the argon is recirculated through a cold charcoal trap that retains essentially all radon entering it, with the full argon inventory passing through it once every 20 days (radon-222 half-life 3.8 days). Radon is dissolved throughout the argon, and its progeny are born as positive ions and collect on the detector surfaces like 42K.
In the same prototype, the contribution at Q from these radon progeny on the detector surfaces (mainly 214Bi, beta endpoint 3.27 MeV), after the same vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 9e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) (radon-progeny gammas are included in the other contributions).
All other contributions at Q are estimated at 1.6e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
The instrument's goal is a total background index at Q below 2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), of which at most 4e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) is allotted to beta decays on or near the detector surfaces.

In a prototype with this array design and argon of atmospheric origin, the 42K contribution at Q, after vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 1.2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
42K (half-life 12.4 h) is the daughter of 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr) and beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly without a coincident gamma; it is born as a positive ion and drifts to the detector surfaces in their electric fields.
The planned instrument uses the prototype's cryostat, argon recirculation system and trap: the radon in the argon is emanated by the cryostat walls and the argon recirculation system, outside the array; the argon is recirculated through a cold charcoal trap that retains essentially all radon entering it, with the full argon inventory passing through it once every 20 days (radon-222 half-life 3.8 days). Radon is dissolved throughout the argon, and its progeny are born as positive ions and collect on the detector surfaces like 42K.
In the same prototype, the contribution at Q from these radon progeny on the detector surfaces (mainly 214Bi, beta endpoint 3.27 MeV), after the same vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 9e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) (radon-progeny gammas are included in the other contributions).
All other contributions at Q are estimated at 1.6e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
The instrument's goal is a total background index at Q below 2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), of which at most 4e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) is allotted to beta decays on or near the detector surfaces.

A planned experiment searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 76Ge (Q = 2039 keV) with 600 kg of enriched germanium detectors, operated bare in strings, in a laboratory at 3500 m water-equivalent depth.
The strings stand in liquid argon inside a cryostat surrounded by a water tank used as a muon veto; argon scintillation light vetoes events that deposit energy in the argon, and germanium pulse-shape analysis rejects multi-site and surface events.
In a prototype with this array design and argon of atmospheric origin, the 42K contribution at Q, after vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 1.2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
42K (half-life 12.4 h) is the daughter of 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr) and beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly without a coincident gamma; it is born as a positive ion and drifts to the detector surfaces in their electric fields.
The planned instrument uses the prototype's cryostat, argon recirculation system and trap: the radon in the argon is emanated by the cryostat walls and the argon recirculation system, outside the array; the argon is recirculated through a cold charcoal trap that retains essentially all radon entering it, with the full argon inventory passing through it once every 20 days (radon-222 half-life 3.8 days). Radon is dissolved throughout the argon, and its progeny are born as positive ions and collect on the detector surfaces like 42K.
In the same prototype, the contribution at Q from these radon progeny on the detector surfaces (mainly 214Bi, beta endpoint 3.27 MeV), after the same vetoes and pulse-shape cuts, was measured at 9e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) (radon-progeny gammas are included in the other contributions).
All other contributions at Q are estimated at 1.6e-5 counts/(keV kg yr).
The instrument's goal is a total background index at Q below 2e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), of which at most 4e-6 counts/(keV kg yr) is allotted to beta decays on or near the detector surfaces.

The following describes a particle-physics detector.

GERDA Phase II searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 76Ge (Q = 2039 keV) at the LNGS underground laboratory.
About 35 kg of enriched germanium detectors (coaxial and broad-energy types) are operated bare, in strings, inside a cryostat holding about 64 m^3 of liquid argon of atmospheric origin, which sits in a water tank instrumented as a muon veto.
The liquid argon is both coolant and shield, and its scintillation light, read out by photomultipliers and wavelength-shifting fibres, vetoes events with energy deposited in the argon.
Pulse-shape analysis of the germanium signals rejects multi-site and surface events.
Argon of atmospheric origin contains 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr); its daughter 42K (half-life 12.4 h) beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly to the ground state without a coincident gamma.
42K is produced as a positive ion and drifts in the electric fields around the detectors, collecting on their surfaces; in this phase the strings are surrounded by thin transparent nylon cylinders.
The background index at Q is about 1e-3 counts/(keV kg yr).
A tonne-scale successor must reach a background index below about 1e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), with beta decays on or near the detector surfaces contributing well below that.

GERDA Phase II searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 76Ge (Q = 2039 keV) at the LNGS underground laboratory.
About 35 kg of enriched germanium detectors (coaxial and broad-energy types) are operated bare, in strings, inside a cryostat holding about 64 m^3 of liquid argon of atmospheric origin, which sits in a water tank instrumented as a muon veto.
The liquid argon is both coolant and shield, and its scintillation light, read out by photomultipliers and wavelength-shifting fibres, vetoes events with energy deposited in the argon.
Pulse-shape analysis of the germanium signals rejects multi-site and surface events.
Argon of atmospheric origin contains 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr); its daughter 42K (half-life 12.4 h) beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly to the ground state without a coincident gamma.
42K is produced as a positive ion and drifts in the electric fields around the detectors, collecting on their surfaces; in this phase the strings are surrounded by thin transparent nylon cylinders.
The background index at Q is about 1e-3 counts/(keV kg yr).
A tonne-scale successor must reach a background index below about 1e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), with beta decays on or near the detector surfaces contributing well below that.

GERDA Phase II searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 76Ge (Q = 2039 keV) at the LNGS underground laboratory.
About 35 kg of enriched germanium detectors (coaxial and broad-energy types) are operated bare, in strings, inside a cryostat holding about 64 m^3 of liquid argon of atmospheric origin, which sits in a water tank instrumented as a muon veto.
The liquid argon is both coolant and shield, and its scintillation light, read out by photomultipliers and wavelength-shifting fibres, vetoes events with energy deposited in the argon.
Pulse-shape analysis of the germanium signals rejects multi-site and surface events.
Argon of atmospheric origin contains 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr); its daughter 42K (half-life 12.4 h) beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly to the ground state without a coincident gamma.
42K is produced as a positive ion and drifts in the electric fields around the detectors, collecting on their surfaces; in this phase the strings are surrounded by thin transparent nylon cylinders.
The background index at Q is about 1e-3 counts/(keV kg yr).
A tonne-scale successor must reach a background index below about 1e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), with beta decays on or near the detector surfaces contributing well below that.

GERDA Phase II searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 76Ge (Q = 2039 keV) at the LNGS underground laboratory.
About 35 kg of enriched germanium detectors (coaxial and broad-energy types) are operated bare, in strings, inside a cryostat holding about 64 m^3 of liquid argon of atmospheric origin, which sits in a water tank instrumented as a muon veto.
The liquid argon is both coolant and shield, and its scintillation light, read out by photomultipliers and wavelength-shifting fibres, vetoes events with energy deposited in the argon.
Pulse-shape analysis of the germanium signals rejects multi-site and surface events.
Argon of atmospheric origin contains 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr); its daughter 42K (half-life 12.4 h) beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly to the ground state without a coincident gamma.
42K is produced as a positive ion and drifts in the electric fields around the detectors, collecting on their surfaces; in this phase the strings are surrounded by thin transparent nylon cylinders.
The background index at Q is about 1e-3 counts/(keV kg yr).
A tonne-scale successor must reach a background index below about 1e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), with beta decays on or near the detector surfaces contributing well below that.

GERDA Phase II searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 76Ge (Q = 2039 keV) at the LNGS underground laboratory.
About 35 kg of enriched germanium detectors (coaxial and broad-energy types) are operated bare, in strings, inside a cryostat holding about 64 m^3 of liquid argon of atmospheric origin, which sits in a water tank instrumented as a muon veto.
The liquid argon is both coolant and shield, and its scintillation light, read out by photomultipliers and wavelength-shifting fibres, vetoes events with energy deposited in the argon.
Pulse-shape analysis of the germanium signals rejects multi-site and surface events.
Argon of atmospheric origin contains 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr); its daughter 42K (half-life 12.4 h) beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly to the ground state without a coincident gamma.
42K is produced as a positive ion and drifts in the electric fields around the detectors, collecting on their surfaces; in this phase the strings are surrounded by thin transparent nylon cylinders.
The background index at Q is about 1e-3 counts/(keV kg yr).
A tonne-scale successor must reach a background index below about 1e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), with beta decays on or near the detector surfaces contributing well below that.

About 35 kg of enriched germanium detectors (coaxial and broad-energy types) are operated bare, in strings, inside a cryostat holding about 64 m^3 of liquid argon of atmospheric origin, which sits in a water tank instrumented as a muon veto.
The liquid argon is both coolant and shield, and its scintillation light, read out by photomultipliers and wavelength-shifting fibres, vetoes events with energy deposited in the argon.
Pulse-shape analysis of the germanium signals rejects multi-site and surface events.
Argon of atmospheric origin contains 42Ar (half-life about 33 yr); its daughter 42K (half-life 12.4 h) beta-decays with a 3.5 MeV endpoint, mostly to the ground state without a coincident gamma.
42K is produced as a positive ion and drifts in the electric fields around the detectors, collecting on their surfaces; in this phase the strings are surrounded by thin transparent nylon cylinders.
The background index at Q is about 1e-3 counts/(keV kg yr).
A tonne-scale successor must reach a background index below about 1e-5 counts/(keV kg yr), with beta decays on or near the detector surfaces contributing well below that.

The following describes a particle-physics detector.

A ground-based laser-interferometric gravitational-wave detector: a dual-recycled Michelson interferometer with 3 km Fabry-Perot arm cavities, operating at 1064 nm.
The test masses are ~42 kg fused-silica mirrors on monolithic suspensions hung from multi-stage seismic isolators.
At the planned arm power the radiation-pressure and shot-noise contributions to quantum noise cross in the few-tens-of-Hz region, inside the detection band.
A squeezed-vacuum source (more than 10 dB of measured quadrature noise reduction at the source) injects into the dark port; the total efficiency from source to output photodetector is a few tens of percent loss.
The site has long evacuated beam tubes in which auxiliary optics up to several hundred metres long can be housed.
Requirement: at the planned arm power, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

A ground-based laser-interferometric gravitational-wave detector: a dual-recycled Michelson interferometer with 3 km Fabry-Perot arm cavities, operating at 1064 nm.
The test masses are ~42 kg fused-silica mirrors on monolithic suspensions hung from multi-stage seismic isolators.
At the planned arm power the radiation-pressure and shot-noise contributions to quantum noise cross in the few-tens-of-Hz region, inside the detection band.
A squeezed-vacuum source (more than 10 dB of measured quadrature noise reduction at the source) injects into the dark port; the total efficiency from source to output photodetector is a few tens of percent loss.
The site has long evacuated beam tubes in which auxiliary optics up to several hundred metres long can be housed.
Requirement: at the planned arm power, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

At the planned arm power the radiation-pressure and shot-noise contributions to quantum noise cross in the few-tens-of-Hz region, inside the detection band.
A squeezed-vacuum source (more than 10 dB of measured quadrature noise reduction at the source) injects into the dark port; the total efficiency from source to output photodetector is a few tens of percent loss.
The site has long evacuated beam tubes in which auxiliary optics up to several hundred metres long can be housed.
Requirement: at the planned arm power, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

The test masses are 55 kg fused-silica mirrors on monolithic suspensions; the main interferometer topology and its operating point, arm power and test-mass mass are fixed as stated.
At the planned arm power, radiation-pressure noise equals shot noise at 55 Hz; below this frequency quantum noise is radiation-pressure dominated, above it shot-noise dominated.
A squeezed-vacuum source delivers 13 dB of quadrature noise reduction at its output; the total optical efficiency from the source, through the interferometer, to the output photodetector is 90%.
The longest straight evacuated beam path available for auxiliary optics at the vertex station is 400 m; no longer path exists or can be added at the site, and no auxiliary optics or separate auxiliary beam lines can be installed in the 3.6 km arm tubes.
The lowest-loss high-reflectivity mirrors available to this project have 5 ppm loss per reflection (absorption plus scatter).
Requirement: at the stated arm power and test-mass mass, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

Propose concrete hardware upgrades for this detector's next phase. For each, name the technology and explain the physics motivation.

The test masses are 55 kg fused-silica mirrors on monolithic suspensions; the main interferometer topology and its operating point, arm power and test-mass mass are fixed as stated.
At the planned arm power, radiation-pressure noise equals shot noise at 55 Hz; below this frequency quantum noise is radiation-pressure dominated, above it shot-noise dominated.
A squeezed-vacuum source delivers 13 dB of quadrature noise reduction at its output; the total optical efficiency from the source, through the interferometer, to the output photodetector is 90%.
The longest straight evacuated beam path available for auxiliary optics at the vertex station is 400 m; no longer path exists or can be added at the site, and no auxiliary optics or separate auxiliary beam lines can be installed in the 3.6 km arm tubes.
The lowest-loss high-reflectivity mirrors available to this project have 5 ppm loss per reflection (absorption plus scatter).
Requirement: at the stated arm power and test-mass mass, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

Propose concrete hardware upgrades for this detector's next phase. For each, name the technology and explain the physics motivation.

The test masses are 55 kg fused-silica mirrors on monolithic suspensions; the main interferometer topology and its operating point, arm power and test-mass mass are fixed as stated.
At the planned arm power, radiation-pressure noise equals shot noise at 55 Hz; below this frequency quantum noise is radiation-pressure dominated, above it shot-noise dominated.
A squeezed-vacuum source delivers 13 dB of quadrature noise reduction at its output; the total optical efficiency from the source, through the interferometer, to the output photodetector is 90%.
The longest straight evacuated beam path available for auxiliary optics at the vertex station is 400 m; no longer path exists or can be added at the site, and no auxiliary optics or separate auxiliary beam lines can be installed in the 3.6 km arm tubes.
The lowest-loss high-reflectivity mirrors available to this project have 5 ppm loss per reflection (absorption plus scatter).
Requirement: at the stated arm power and test-mass mass, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

Propose concrete hardware upgrades for this detector's next phase. For each, name the technology and explain the physics motivation.

The test masses are 55 kg fused-silica mirrors on monolithic suspensions; the main interferometer topology and its operating point, arm power and test-mass mass are fixed as stated.
At the planned arm power, radiation-pressure noise equals shot noise at 55 Hz; below this frequency quantum noise is radiation-pressure dominated, above it shot-noise dominated.
A squeezed-vacuum source delivers 13 dB of quadrature noise reduction at its output; the total optical efficiency from the source, through the interferometer, to the output photodetector is 90%.
The longest straight evacuated beam path available for auxiliary optics at the vertex station is 400 m; no longer path exists or can be added at the site, and no auxiliary optics or separate auxiliary beam lines can be installed in the 3.6 km arm tubes.
The lowest-loss high-reflectivity mirrors available to this project have 5 ppm loss per reflection (absorption plus scatter).
Requirement: at the stated arm power and test-mass mass, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

The test masses are 55 kg fused-silica mirrors on monolithic suspensions; the main interferometer topology and its operating point, arm power and test-mass mass are fixed as stated.
At the planned arm power, radiation-pressure noise equals shot noise at 55 Hz; below this frequency quantum noise is radiation-pressure dominated, above it shot-noise dominated.
A squeezed-vacuum source delivers 13 dB of quadrature noise reduction at its output; the total optical efficiency from the source, through the interferometer, to the output photodetector is 90%.
The longest straight evacuated beam path available for auxiliary optics at the vertex station is 400 m; no longer path exists or can be added at the site, and no auxiliary optics or separate auxiliary beam lines can be installed in the 3.6 km arm tubes.
The lowest-loss high-reflectivity mirrors available to this project have 5 ppm loss per reflection (absorption plus scatter).
Requirement: at the stated arm power and test-mass mass, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

The test masses are 55 kg fused-silica mirrors on monolithic suspensions; the main interferometer topology and its operating point, arm power and test-mass mass are fixed as stated.
At the planned arm power, radiation-pressure noise equals shot noise at 55 Hz; below this frequency quantum noise is radiation-pressure dominated, above it shot-noise dominated.
A squeezed-vacuum source delivers 13 dB of quadrature noise reduction at its output; the total optical efficiency from the source, through the interferometer, to the output photodetector is 90%.
The longest straight evacuated beam path available for auxiliary optics at the vertex station is 8 m; no longer path exists or can be added at the site, and no auxiliary optics or separate auxiliary beam lines can be installed in the 3.6 km arm tubes.
The lowest-loss high-reflectivity mirrors available to this project have 5 ppm loss per reflection (absorption plus scatter).
Requirement: at the stated arm power and test-mass mass, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

Propose concrete hardware upgrades for this detector's next phase. For each, name the technology and explain the physics motivation.

The test masses are 55 kg fused-silica mirrors on monolithic suspensions; the main interferometer topology and its operating point, arm power and test-mass mass are fixed as stated.
At the planned arm power, radiation-pressure noise equals shot noise at 55 Hz; below this frequency quantum noise is radiation-pressure dominated, above it shot-noise dominated.
A squeezed-vacuum source delivers 13 dB of quadrature noise reduction at its output; the total optical efficiency from the source, through the interferometer, to the output photodetector is 90%.
The longest straight evacuated beam path available for auxiliary optics at the vertex station is 8 m; no longer path exists or can be added at the site, and no auxiliary optics or separate auxiliary beam lines can be installed in the 3.6 km arm tubes.
The lowest-loss high-reflectivity mirrors available to this project have 5 ppm loss per reflection (absorption plus scatter).
Requirement: at the stated arm power and test-mass mass, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

Propose concrete hardware upgrades for this detector's next phase. For each, name the technology and explain the physics motivation.

The test masses are 55 kg fused-silica mirrors on monolithic suspensions; the main interferometer topology and its operating point, arm power and test-mass mass are fixed as stated.
At the planned arm power, radiation-pressure noise equals shot noise at 55 Hz; below this frequency quantum noise is radiation-pressure dominated, above it shot-noise dominated.
A squeezed-vacuum source delivers 13 dB of quadrature noise reduction at its output; the total optical efficiency from the source, through the interferometer, to the output photodetector is 90%.
The longest straight evacuated beam path available for auxiliary optics at the vertex station is 8 m; no longer path exists or can be added at the site, and no auxiliary optics or separate auxiliary beam lines can be installed in the 3.6 km arm tubes.
The lowest-loss high-reflectivity mirrors available to this project have 5 ppm loss per reflection (absorption plus scatter).
Requirement: at the stated arm power and test-mass mass, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

Propose concrete hardware upgrades for this detector's next phase. For each, name the technology and explain the physics motivation.

End your answer with one line of the form:

At the planned arm power, radiation-pressure noise equals shot noise at 55 Hz; below this frequency quantum noise is radiation-pressure dominated, above it shot-noise dominated.
A squeezed-vacuum source delivers 13 dB of quadrature noise reduction at its output; the total optical efficiency from the source, through the interferometer, to the output photodetector is 90%.
The longest straight evacuated beam path available for auxiliary optics at the vertex station is 8 m; no longer path exists or can be added at the site, and no auxiliary optics or separate auxiliary beam lines can be installed in the 3.6 km arm tubes.
The lowest-loss high-reflectivity mirrors available to this project have 5 ppm loss per reflection (absorption plus scatter).
Requirement: at the stated arm power and test-mass mass, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

List the hardware upgrades the proposal should include, with the specific technology for each and why.

At the planned arm power, radiation-pressure noise equals shot noise at 55 Hz; below this frequency quantum noise is radiation-pressure dominated, above it shot-noise dominated.
A squeezed-vacuum source delivers 13 dB of quadrature noise reduction at its output; the total optical efficiency from the source, through the interferometer, to the output photodetector is 90%.
The longest straight evacuated beam path available for auxiliary optics at the vertex station is 8 m; no longer path exists or can be added at the site, and no auxiliary optics or separate auxiliary beam lines can be installed in the 3.6 km arm tubes.
The lowest-loss high-reflectivity mirrors available to this project have 5 ppm loss per reflection (absorption plus scatter).
Requirement: at the stated arm power and test-mass mass, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

List the hardware upgrades the proposal should include, with the specific technology for each and why.
