At the planned arm power, radiation-pressure noise equals shot noise at 55 Hz; below this frequency quantum noise is radiation-pressure dominated, above it shot-noise dominated.
A squeezed-vacuum source delivers 13 dB of quadrature noise reduction at its output; the total optical efficiency from the source, through the interferometer, to the output photodetector is 90%.
The longest straight evacuated beam path available for auxiliary optics at the vertex station is 8 m; no longer path exists or can be added at the site, and no auxiliary optics or separate auxiliary beam lines can be installed in the 3.6 km arm tubes.
The lowest-loss high-reflectivity mirrors available to this project have 5 ppm loss per reflection (absorption plus scatter).
Requirement: at the stated arm power and test-mass mass, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

List the hardware upgrades the proposal should include, with the specific technology for each and why.

At the planned arm power, radiation-pressure noise equals shot noise at 55 Hz; below this frequency quantum noise is radiation-pressure dominated, above it shot-noise dominated.
A squeezed-vacuum source delivers 13 dB of quadrature noise reduction at its output; the total optical efficiency from the source, through the interferometer, to the output photodetector is 90%.
The longest straight evacuated beam path available for auxiliary optics at the vertex station is 8 m; no longer path exists or can be added at the site, and no auxiliary optics or separate auxiliary beam lines can be installed in the 3.6 km arm tubes.
The lowest-loss high-reflectivity mirrors available to this project have 5 ppm loss per reflection (absorption plus scatter).
Requirement: at the stated arm power and test-mass mass, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

Requirement: at the stated arm power and test-mass mass, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

The test masses are 55 kg fused-silica mirrors on monolithic suspensions; the main interferometer topology and its operating point, arm power and test-mass mass are fixed as stated.
At the planned arm power, radiation-pressure noise equals shot noise at 55 Hz; below this frequency quantum noise is radiation-pressure dominated, above it shot-noise dominated.
A squeezed-vacuum source delivers 13 dB of quadrature noise reduction at its output; the total optical efficiency from the source, through the interferometer, to the output photodetector is 90%.
The longest straight evacuated beam path available for auxiliary optics at the vertex station is 8 m; no longer path exists or can be added at the site, and no auxiliary optics or separate auxiliary beam lines can be installed in the 3.6 km arm tubes.
The lowest-loss high-reflectivity mirrors available to this project have 5 ppm loss per reflection (absorption plus scatter).
Requirement: at the stated arm power and test-mass mass, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

The following describes a particle-physics detector.

Advanced Virgo (AdV), the upgraded Virgo gravitational-wave detector at the EGO site in Cascina, Italy, in its AdV+ Phase I configuration.
It is a dual-recycled Michelson interferometer with 3 km Fabry-Perot arm cavities, operating at 1064 nm, with ~42 kg fused-silica test masses on monolithic suspensions hung from multi-stage seismic isolators.
At the planned arm power the radiation-pressure and shot-noise contributions to quantum noise cross in the few-tens-of-Hz region, inside the detection band.
A squeezed-vacuum source (more than 10 dB of measured quadrature noise reduction at the source) injects into the dark port; the total efficiency from source to output photodetector is a few tens of percent loss.
The site has long evacuated beam tubes in which auxiliary optics up to several hundred metres long can be housed.
Requirement: at the planned arm power, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

Propose concrete hardware upgrades for this detector's next phase. For each, name the technology and explain the physics motivation.

Advanced Virgo (AdV), the upgraded Virgo gravitational-wave detector at the EGO site in Cascina, Italy, in its AdV+ Phase I configuration.
It is a dual-recycled Michelson interferometer with 3 km Fabry-Perot arm cavities, operating at 1064 nm, with ~42 kg fused-silica test masses on monolithic suspensions hung from multi-stage seismic isolators.
At the planned arm power the radiation-pressure and shot-noise contributions to quantum noise cross in the few-tens-of-Hz region, inside the detection band.
A squeezed-vacuum source (more than 10 dB of measured quadrature noise reduction at the source) injects into the dark port; the total efficiency from source to output photodetector is a few tens of percent loss.
The site has long evacuated beam tubes in which auxiliary optics up to several hundred metres long can be housed.
Requirement: at the planned arm power, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

It is a dual-recycled Michelson interferometer with 3 km Fabry-Perot arm cavities, operating at 1064 nm, with ~42 kg fused-silica test masses on monolithic suspensions hung from multi-stage seismic isolators.
At the planned arm power the radiation-pressure and shot-noise contributions to quantum noise cross in the few-tens-of-Hz region, inside the detection band.
A squeezed-vacuum source (more than 10 dB of measured quadrature noise reduction at the source) injects into the dark port; the total efficiency from source to output photodetector is a few tens of percent loss.
The site has long evacuated beam tubes in which auxiliary optics up to several hundred metres long can be housed.
Requirement: at the planned arm power, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

It is a dual-recycled Michelson interferometer with 3 km Fabry-Perot arm cavities, operating at 1064 nm, with ~42 kg fused-silica test masses on monolithic suspensions hung from multi-stage seismic isolators.
At the planned arm power the radiation-pressure and shot-noise contributions to quantum noise cross in the few-tens-of-Hz region, inside the detection band.
A squeezed-vacuum source (more than 10 dB of measured quadrature noise reduction at the source) injects into the dark port; the total efficiency from source to output photodetector is a few tens of percent loss.
The site has long evacuated beam tubes in which auxiliary optics up to several hundred metres long can be housed.
Requirement: at the planned arm power, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

Advanced Virgo (AdV), the upgraded Virgo gravitational-wave detector at the EGO site in Cascina, Italy, in its AdV+ Phase I configuration.
It is a dual-recycled Michelson interferometer with 3 km Fabry-Perot arm cavities, operating at 1064 nm, with ~42 kg fused-silica test masses on monolithic suspensions hung from multi-stage seismic isolators.
At the planned arm power the radiation-pressure and shot-noise contributions to quantum noise cross in the few-tens-of-Hz region, inside the detection band.
A squeezed-vacuum source (more than 10 dB of measured quadrature noise reduction at the source) injects into the dark port; the total efficiency from source to output photodetector is a few tens of percent loss.
The site has long evacuated beam tubes in which auxiliary optics up to several hundred metres long can be housed.
Requirement: at the planned arm power, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

It is a dual-recycled Michelson interferometer with 3 km Fabry-Perot arm cavities, operating at 1064 nm, with ~42 kg fused-silica test masses on monolithic suspensions hung from multi-stage seismic isolators.
At the planned arm power the radiation-pressure and shot-noise contributions to quantum noise cross in the few-tens-of-Hz region, inside the detection band.
A squeezed-vacuum source (more than 10 dB of measured quadrature noise reduction at the source) injects into the dark port; the total efficiency from source to output photodetector is a few tens of percent loss.
The site has long evacuated beam tubes in which auxiliary optics up to several hundred metres long can be housed.
Requirement: at the planned arm power, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

It is a dual-recycled Michelson interferometer with 3 km Fabry-Perot arm cavities, operating at 1064 nm, with ~42 kg fused-silica test masses on monolithic suspensions hung from multi-stage seismic isolators.
At the planned arm power the radiation-pressure and shot-noise contributions to quantum noise cross in the few-tens-of-Hz region, inside the detection band.
A squeezed-vacuum source (more than 10 dB of measured quadrature noise reduction at the source) injects into the dark port; the total efficiency from source to output photodetector is a few tens of percent loss.
The site has long evacuated beam tubes in which auxiliary optics up to several hundred metres long can be housed.
Requirement: at the planned arm power, the next phase must lower total quantum noise by at least 3 dB at every frequency from 20 Hz to 800 Hz, relative to the quantum noise of the interferometer with ordinary vacuum entering its output port.

The following describes a particle-physics detector.

An underground neutrino detector sits about 2 km below the surface (about 6,000 m water equivalent) in an active mine.
Its target is 1,000 tonnes of heavy water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 12 m diameter with a 5.5 cm wall. The sphere hangs from ropes attached to a deck above the cavity.
About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

Its target is 1,000 tonnes of heavy water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 12 m diameter with a 5.5 cm wall. The sphere hangs from ropes attached to a deck above the cavity.
About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

Its target is 1,000 tonnes of heavy water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 12 m diameter with a 5.5 cm wall. The sphere hangs from ropes attached to a deck above the cavity.
About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

An underground neutrino detector sits about 2 km below the surface (about 6,000 m water equivalent) in an active mine.
Its target is 1,000 tonnes of heavy water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 12 m diameter with a 5.5 cm wall. The sphere hangs from ropes attached to a deck above the cavity.
About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

An underground neutrino detector sits about 2 km below the surface (about 6,000 m water equivalent) in an active mine.
Its target is 1,000 tonnes of heavy water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 12 m diameter with a 5.5 cm wall. The sphere hangs from ropes attached to a deck above the cavity.
About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

Its target is 1,000 tonnes of heavy water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 12 m diameter with a 5.5 cm wall. The sphere hangs from ropes attached to a deck above the cavity.
About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

Its target is 1,000 tonnes of heavy water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 12 m diameter with a 5.5 cm wall. The sphere hangs from ropes attached to a deck above the cavity.
About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

Its target is 1,000 tonnes of heavy water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 12 m diameter with a 5.5 cm wall. The sphere hangs from ropes attached to a deck above the cavity.
About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

An underground neutrino detector sits 1.6 km below the surface in a mine cavity.
Its target is 520 tonnes of ultrapure light water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 10 m diameter with a 5 cm wall. The water inside the sphere is kept separate from the shield water outside it.
About 6,800 10-inch photomultiplier tubes on a support frame of 16 m diameter view the sphere. The cavity around the sphere and the tubes is filled with 4,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which acts as the shield.
The detector currently records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos above about 4 MeV. It collects roughly 8 photoelectrons per MeV.
The next programme targets pep and CNO solar neutrinos, geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos. It reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water.

On average, 12% of the photons emitted isotropically inside the sphere produce a photoelectron in the array.
The next programme requires at least 400 photoelectrons per MeV of energy deposited inside the sphere.
The sphere wall, counting its own weight, withstands a net vertical load, upward or downward, of at most 300 kg per cubic metre of contained volume, however the sphere is restrained.

Its target is 520 tonnes of ultrapure light water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 10 m diameter with a 5 cm wall. The water inside the sphere is kept separate from the shield water outside it.
About 6,800 10-inch photomultiplier tubes on a support frame of 16 m diameter view the sphere. The cavity around the sphere and the tubes is filled with 4,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which acts as the shield.
The detector currently records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos above about 4 MeV. It collects roughly 8 photoelectrons per MeV.
The next programme targets pep and CNO solar neutrinos, geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos. It reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water.
The acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water are retained. The sphere sits entirely in the shield water.
On average, 12% of the photons emitted isotropically inside the sphere produce a photoelectron in the array.
The next programme requires at least 400 photoelectrons per MeV of energy deposited inside the sphere.
The sphere wall, counting its own weight, withstands a net vertical load, upward or downward, of at most 300 kg per cubic metre of contained volume, however the sphere is restrained.

Propose concrete hardware upgrades for this detector's next phase. For each, name the technology and explain the physics motivation.

End your answer with one line of the form:

An underground neutrino detector sits 1.6 km below the surface in a mine cavity.
Its target is 520 tonnes of ultrapure light water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 10 m diameter with a 5 cm wall. The water inside the sphere is kept separate from the shield water outside it.
About 6,800 10-inch photomultiplier tubes on a support frame of 16 m diameter view the sphere. The cavity around the sphere and the tubes is filled with 4,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which acts as the shield.
The detector currently records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos above about 4 MeV. It collects roughly 8 photoelectrons per MeV.
The next programme targets pep and CNO solar neutrinos, geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos. It reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water.
The acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water are retained. The sphere sits entirely in the shield water.
On average, 12% of the photons emitted isotropically inside the sphere produce a photoelectron in the array.
The next programme requires at least 400 photoelectrons per MeV of energy deposited inside the sphere.
The sphere wall, counting its own weight, withstands a net vertical load, upward or downward, of at most 300 kg per cubic metre of contained volume, however the sphere is restrained.

Its target is 520 tonnes of ultrapure light water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 10 m diameter with a 5 cm wall. The water inside the sphere is kept separate from the shield water outside it.
About 6,800 10-inch photomultiplier tubes on a support frame of 16 m diameter view the sphere. The cavity around the sphere and the tubes is filled with 4,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which acts as the shield.
The detector currently records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos above about 4 MeV. It collects roughly 8 photoelectrons per MeV.
The next programme targets pep and CNO solar neutrinos, geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos. It reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water.
The acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water are retained. The sphere sits entirely in the shield water.
On average, 12% of the photons emitted isotropically inside the sphere produce a photoelectron in the array.
The next programme requires at least 400 photoelectrons per MeV of energy deposited inside the sphere.
The sphere wall, counting its own weight, withstands a net vertical load, upward or downward, of at most 300 kg per cubic metre of contained volume, however the sphere is restrained.

About 6,800 10-inch photomultiplier tubes on a support frame of 16 m diameter view the sphere. The cavity around the sphere and the tubes is filled with 4,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which acts as the shield.
The detector currently records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos above about 4 MeV. It collects roughly 8 photoelectrons per MeV.
The next programme targets pep and CNO solar neutrinos, geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos. It reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water.
The acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water are retained. The sphere sits entirely in the shield water.
On average, 12% of the photons emitted isotropically inside the sphere produce a photoelectron in the array.
The next programme requires at least 400 photoelectrons per MeV of energy deposited inside the sphere.
The sphere wall, counting its own weight, withstands a net vertical load, upward or downward, of at most 300 kg per cubic metre of contained volume, however the sphere is restrained.

Its target is 520 tonnes of ultrapure light water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 10 m diameter with a 1 cm wall. The water inside the sphere is kept separate from the shield water outside it.
About 6,800 10-inch photomultiplier tubes on a support frame of 16 m diameter view the sphere. The cavity around the sphere and the tubes is filled with 4,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which acts as the shield.
The detector currently records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos above about 4 MeV. It collects roughly 8 photoelectrons per MeV.
The next programme targets pep and CNO solar neutrinos, geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos. It reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water.
The acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water are retained. The sphere sits entirely in the shield water.
On average, 12% of the photons emitted isotropically inside the sphere produce a photoelectron in the array.
The next programme requires at least 400 photoelectrons per MeV of energy deposited inside the sphere.
The sphere wall, counting its own weight, withstands a net vertical load, upward or downward, of at most 60 kg per cubic metre of contained volume, however the sphere is restrained.

Propose concrete hardware upgrades for this detector's next phase. For each, name the technology and explain the physics motivation.

End your answer with one line of the form:

An underground neutrino detector sits 1.6 km below the surface in a mine cavity.
Its target is 520 tonnes of ultrapure light water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 10 m diameter with a 1 cm wall. The water inside the sphere is kept separate from the shield water outside it.
About 6,800 10-inch photomultiplier tubes on a support frame of 16 m diameter view the sphere. The cavity around the sphere and the tubes is filled with 4,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which acts as the shield.
The detector currently records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos above about 4 MeV. It collects roughly 8 photoelectrons per MeV.
The next programme targets pep and CNO solar neutrinos, geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos. It reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water.
The acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water are retained. The sphere sits entirely in the shield water.
On average, 12% of the photons emitted isotropically inside the sphere produce a photoelectron in the array.
The next programme requires at least 400 photoelectrons per MeV of energy deposited inside the sphere.
The sphere wall, counting its own weight, withstands a net vertical load, upward or downward, of at most 60 kg per cubic metre of contained volume, however the sphere is restrained.

An underground neutrino detector sits 1.6 km below the surface in a mine cavity.
Its target is 520 tonnes of ultrapure light water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 10 m diameter with a 1 cm wall. The water inside the sphere is kept separate from the shield water outside it.
About 6,800 10-inch photomultiplier tubes on a support frame of 16 m diameter view the sphere. The cavity around the sphere and the tubes is filled with 4,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which acts as the shield.
The detector currently records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos above about 4 MeV. It collects roughly 8 photoelectrons per MeV.
The next programme targets pep and CNO solar neutrinos, geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos. It reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water.
The acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water are retained. The sphere sits entirely in the shield water.
On average, 12% of the photons emitted isotropically inside the sphere produce a photoelectron in the array.
The next programme requires at least 400 photoelectrons per MeV of energy deposited inside the sphere.
The sphere wall, counting its own weight, withstands a net vertical load, upward or downward, of at most 60 kg per cubic metre of contained volume, however the sphere is restrained.

An underground neutrino detector sits 1.6 km below the surface in a mine cavity.
Its target is 520 tonnes of ultrapure light water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 10 m diameter with a 1 cm wall. The water inside the sphere is kept separate from the shield water outside it.
About 6,800 10-inch photomultiplier tubes on a support frame of 16 m diameter view the sphere. The cavity around the sphere and the tubes is filled with 4,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which acts as the shield.
The detector currently records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos above about 4 MeV. It collects roughly 8 photoelectrons per MeV.
The next programme targets pep and CNO solar neutrinos, geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos. It reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water.
The acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water are retained. The sphere sits entirely in the shield water.
On average, 12% of the photons emitted isotropically inside the sphere produce a photoelectron in the array.
The next programme requires at least 400 photoelectrons per MeV of energy deposited inside the sphere.
The sphere wall, counting its own weight, withstands a net vertical load, upward or downward, of at most 60 kg per cubic metre of contained volume, however the sphere is restrained.

Its target is 520 tonnes of ultrapure light water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 10 m diameter with a 1 cm wall. The water inside the sphere is kept separate from the shield water outside it.
About 6,800 10-inch photomultiplier tubes on a support frame of 16 m diameter view the sphere. The cavity around the sphere and the tubes is filled with 4,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which acts as the shield.
The detector currently records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos above about 4 MeV. It collects roughly 8 photoelectrons per MeV.
The next programme targets pep and CNO solar neutrinos, geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos. It reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water.
The acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the shield water are retained. The sphere sits entirely in the shield water.
On average, 12% of the photons emitted isotropically inside the sphere produce a photoelectron in the array.
The next programme requires at least 400 photoelectrons per MeV of energy deposited inside the sphere.
The sphere wall, counting its own weight, withstands a net vertical load, upward or downward, of at most 60 kg per cubic metre of contained volume, however the sphere is restrained.

About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

The Sudbury Neutrino Observatory (SNO) sits 2,092 m underground (about 6,000 m water equivalent) in the Creighton mine near Sudbury, Canada.
Its target is 1,000 tonnes of heavy water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 12 m diameter with a 5.5 cm wall. The sphere hangs from ropes attached to a deck above the cavity.
About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

The Sudbury Neutrino Observatory (SNO) sits 2,092 m underground (about 6,000 m water equivalent) in the Creighton mine near Sudbury, Canada.
Its target is 1,000 tonnes of heavy water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 12 m diameter with a 5.5 cm wall. The sphere hangs from ropes attached to a deck above the cavity.
About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.

About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

Its target is 1,000 tonnes of heavy water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 12 m diameter with a 5.5 cm wall. The sphere hangs from ropes attached to a deck above the cavity.
About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

The Sudbury Neutrino Observatory (SNO) sits 2,092 m underground (about 6,000 m water equivalent) in the Creighton mine near Sudbury, Canada.
Its target is 1,000 tonnes of heavy water held in a transparent acrylic sphere of 12 m diameter with a 5.5 cm wall. The sphere hangs from ropes attached to a deck above the cavity.
About 9,500 8-inch photomultiplier tubes, mounted on a 17.8 m diameter geodesic structure, view the sphere. The cavity is filled with about 7,000 tonnes of ultrapure light water, which shields the target and surrounds both the sphere and the tubes.
The detector records Cherenkov light from 8B solar neutrinos through charged-current, neutral-current and elastic-scattering reactions on deuterium and electrons. Its analysis threshold is a few MeV.
With the heavy-water programme finished, the collaboration plans a follow-on programme that reuses the cavity, the acrylic sphere, the photomultiplier array and the light-water shield.
The follow-on programme targets solar neutrinos well below 1 MeV (pep and CNO), geoneutrinos and reactor antineutrinos, and a search for neutrinoless double-beta decay.
These goals require visible energies down to a few hundred keV, with an energy resolution of a few percent near 1 MeV.
The heavy water is returned after the heavy-water programme. The acrylic sphere, photomultiplier array and light-water shield are retained.

The following describes a particle-physics detector.

A tracker-calorimeter double-beta-decay experiment is operated in a deep underground laboratory.
About 10 kg of enriched isotopes (mostly 100Mo, also 82Se, 116Cd, 130Te, 150Nd, 96Zr, 48Ca) are rolled into thin source foils arranged in a cylinder of 20 sectors.
On both sides of the foils, 6180 open drift cells operated in Geiger mode reconstruct each electron track in a 25 G solenoidal field, which separates electrons from positrons.
The tracking volume is closed by calorimeter walls of 1940 polystyrene-based plastic scintillator blocks, about 10 cm thick, each coupled, mostly through a light guide, to a low-radioactivity 3-in. or 5-in. photomultiplier.
The calorimeter reaches an energy resolution of 14-17% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of about 250 ps at 1 MeV.
Iron, water and wood shielding surround the detector, which sits under about 4800 m water equivalent of rock.
The follow-up detector will hold about 100 kg of isotope in the same tracker-calorimeter layout and aims at a half-life sensitivity near 1e26 years.
It requires an energy resolution of about 8% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons in every calorimeter cell.
It requires a time resolution of about 400 ps at 1 MeV between two cells, to reject electrons crossing the detector from outside.
Each electron of a decay must have its energy measured individually, and all calorimeter materials must keep 208Tl and 214Bi activity low enough for a 3 MeV region of interest.

About 10 kg of enriched isotopes (mostly 100Mo, also 82Se, 116Cd, 130Te, 150Nd, 96Zr, 48Ca) are rolled into thin source foils arranged in a cylinder of 20 sectors.
On both sides of the foils, 6180 open drift cells operated in Geiger mode reconstruct each electron track in a 25 G solenoidal field, which separates electrons from positrons.
The tracking volume is closed by calorimeter walls of 1940 polystyrene-based plastic scintillator blocks, about 10 cm thick, each coupled, mostly through a light guide, to a low-radioactivity 3-in. or 5-in. photomultiplier.
The calorimeter reaches an energy resolution of 14-17% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of about 250 ps at 1 MeV.
Iron, water and wood shielding surround the detector, which sits under about 4800 m water equivalent of rock.
The follow-up detector will hold about 100 kg of isotope in the same tracker-calorimeter layout and aims at a half-life sensitivity near 1e26 years.
It requires an energy resolution of about 8% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons in every calorimeter cell.
It requires a time resolution of about 400 ps at 1 MeV between two cells, to reject electrons crossing the detector from outside.
Each electron of a decay must have its energy measured individually, and all calorimeter materials must keep 208Tl and 214Bi activity low enough for a 3 MeV region of interest.

Recommend the hardware changes the collaboration should make, naming specific technologies and justifying each.

A tracker-calorimeter double-beta-decay experiment is operated in a deep underground laboratory.
About 10 kg of enriched isotopes (mostly 100Mo, also 82Se, 116Cd, 130Te, 150Nd, 96Zr, 48Ca) are rolled into thin source foils arranged in a cylinder of 20 sectors.
On both sides of the foils, 6180 open drift cells operated in Geiger mode reconstruct each electron track in a 25 G solenoidal field, which separates electrons from positrons.
The tracking volume is closed by calorimeter walls of 1940 polystyrene-based plastic scintillator blocks, about 10 cm thick, each coupled, mostly through a light guide, to a low-radioactivity 3-in. or 5-in. photomultiplier.
The calorimeter reaches an energy resolution of 14-17% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of about 250 ps at 1 MeV.
Iron, water and wood shielding surround the detector, which sits under about 4800 m water equivalent of rock.
The follow-up detector will hold about 100 kg of isotope in the same tracker-calorimeter layout and aims at a half-life sensitivity near 1e26 years.
It requires an energy resolution of about 8% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons in every calorimeter cell.
It requires a time resolution of about 400 ps at 1 MeV between two cells, to reject electrons crossing the detector from outside.
Each electron of a decay must have its energy measured individually, and all calorimeter materials must keep 208Tl and 214Bi activity low enough for a 3 MeV region of interest.

The tracking volume is closed by calorimeter walls of 1940 polystyrene-based plastic scintillator blocks, about 10 cm thick, each coupled, mostly through a light guide, to a low-radioactivity 3-in. or 5-in. photomultiplier.
The calorimeter reaches an energy resolution of 14-17% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of about 250 ps at 1 MeV.
Iron, water and wood shielding surround the detector, which sits under about 4800 m water equivalent of rock.

It requires a time resolution of about 400 ps at 1 MeV between two cells, to reject electrons crossing the detector from outside.
Each electron of a decay must have its energy measured individually, and all calorimeter materials must keep 208Tl and 214Bi activity low enough for a 3 MeV region of interest.

About 10 kg of enriched isotopes (mostly 100Mo, also 82Se, 116Cd, 130Te, 150Nd, 96Zr, 48Ca) are rolled into thin source foils arranged in a cylinder of 20 sectors.
On both sides of the foils, 6180 open drift cells operated in Geiger mode reconstruct each electron track in a 25 G solenoidal field, which separates electrons from positrons.
The tracking volume is closed by calorimeter walls of 1940 polystyrene-based plastic scintillator blocks, about 10 cm thick, each coupled, mostly through a light guide, to a low-radioactivity 3-in. or 5-in. photomultiplier.
The calorimeter reaches an energy resolution of 14-17% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of about 250 ps at 1 MeV.
Iron, water and wood shielding surround the detector, which sits under about 4800 m water equivalent of rock.
The follow-up detector will hold about 100 kg of isotope in the same tracker-calorimeter layout and aims at a half-life sensitivity near 1e26 years.
It requires an energy resolution of about 8% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons in every calorimeter cell.
It requires a time resolution of about 400 ps at 1 MeV between two cells, to reject electrons crossing the detector from outside.
Each electron of a decay must have its energy measured individually, and all calorimeter materials must keep 208Tl and 214Bi activity low enough for a 3 MeV region of interest.

A tracker-calorimeter double-beta-decay experiment is operated in a deep underground laboratory.
About 10 kg of enriched isotopes (mostly 100Mo, also 82Se, 116Cd, 130Te, 150Nd, 96Zr, 48Ca) are rolled into thin source foils arranged in a cylinder of 20 sectors.
On both sides of the foils, 6180 open drift cells operated in Geiger mode reconstruct each electron track in a 25 G solenoidal field, which separates electrons from positrons.
The tracking volume is closed by calorimeter walls of 1940 polystyrene-based plastic scintillator blocks, about 10 cm thick, each coupled, mostly through a light guide, to a low-radioactivity 3-in. or 5-in. photomultiplier.
The calorimeter reaches an energy resolution of 14-17% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of about 250 ps at 1 MeV.
Iron, water and wood shielding surround the detector, which sits under about 4800 m water equivalent of rock.
The follow-up detector will hold about 100 kg of isotope in the same tracker-calorimeter layout and aims at a half-life sensitivity near 1e26 years.
It requires an energy resolution of about 8% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons in every calorimeter cell.
It requires a time resolution of about 400 ps at 1 MeV between two cells, to reject electrons crossing the detector from outside.
Each electron of a decay must have its energy measured individually, and all calorimeter materials must keep 208Tl and 214Bi activity low enough for a 3 MeV region of interest.

The following describes a particle-physics detector.

A planar tracker-calorimeter detector searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 100Mo (Q = 3.03 MeV) in an underground laboratory under 3000 m water equivalent of rock.
About 9 kg of enriched molybdenum is made into foils of 45 mg/cm2 hung in a single vertical plane, 6 m long and 3.5 m high.
On each side of the plane a tracking volume 50 cm deep, filled with Geiger-mode drift cells in a helium-based gas, reconstructs every electron track and its vertex on the foil.
A 3 mT magnetic field parallel to the foil plane fills both tracking volumes and curves the tracks so that electrons are told apart from positrons; the track curvature determines only the sign of the charge.
Each tracking volume is closed by a calorimeter wall of polystyrene scintillator cells with 19 cm x 19 cm faces and 11 cm depth, each viewed through a 30 cm acrylic light guide by a 76 mm photomultiplier sitting behind an iron plate.
The present cells give an energy resolution of 20% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of 0.30 ns (sigma) at 1 MeV.
The detector is enclosed in iron and water shielding, and the gas is flushed to keep radon out of the tracking volumes.
The calorimeter must give an energy resolution of 18% FWHM or better for 1 MeV electrons in every cell.
The calorimeter must give a time resolution of 0.6 ns (sigma) or better at 1 MeV, to reject electrons that cross the detector from outside.
The energy of each electron of a decay is used individually: any two electrons entering a wall at points at least 40 cm apart must deposit their energy in different cells, whose energies are measured separately.
Every cell must be at least 3 cm deep so that it fully absorbs 3 MeV electrons, and every part of the calorimeter must work in the 3 mT field.

About 9 kg of enriched molybdenum is made into foils of 45 mg/cm2 hung in a single vertical plane, 6 m long and 3.5 m high.
On each side of the plane a tracking volume 50 cm deep, filled with Geiger-mode drift cells in a helium-based gas, reconstructs every electron track and its vertex on the foil.
A 3 mT magnetic field parallel to the foil plane fills both tracking volumes and curves the tracks so that electrons are told apart from positrons; the track curvature determines only the sign of the charge.
Each tracking volume is closed by a calorimeter wall of polystyrene scintillator cells with 19 cm x 19 cm faces and 11 cm depth, each viewed through a 30 cm acrylic light guide by a 76 mm photomultiplier sitting behind an iron plate.
The present cells give an energy resolution of 20% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of 0.30 ns (sigma) at 1 MeV.
The detector is enclosed in iron and water shielding, and the gas is flushed to keep radon out of the tracking volumes.
The calorimeter must give an energy resolution of 18% FWHM or better for 1 MeV electrons in every cell.
The calorimeter must give a time resolution of 0.6 ns (sigma) or better at 1 MeV, to reject electrons that cross the detector from outside.
The energy of each electron of a decay is used individually: any two electrons entering a wall at points at least 40 cm apart must deposit their energy in different cells, whose energies are measured separately.
Every cell must be at least 3 cm deep so that it fully absorbs 3 MeV electrons, and every part of the calorimeter must work in the 3 mT field.

A planar tracker-calorimeter detector searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 100Mo (Q = 3.03 MeV) in an underground laboratory under 3000 m water equivalent of rock.
About 9 kg of enriched molybdenum is made into foils of 45 mg/cm2 hung in a single vertical plane, 6 m long and 3.5 m high.
On each side of the plane a tracking volume 50 cm deep, filled with Geiger-mode drift cells in a helium-based gas, reconstructs every electron track and its vertex on the foil.
A 3 mT magnetic field parallel to the foil plane fills both tracking volumes and curves the tracks so that electrons are told apart from positrons; the track curvature determines only the sign of the charge.
Each tracking volume is closed by a calorimeter wall of polystyrene scintillator cells with 19 cm x 19 cm faces and 11 cm depth, each viewed through a 30 cm acrylic light guide by a 76 mm photomultiplier sitting behind an iron plate.
The present cells give an energy resolution of 20% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of 0.30 ns (sigma) at 1 MeV.
The detector is enclosed in iron and water shielding, and the gas is flushed to keep radon out of the tracking volumes.
The calorimeter must give an energy resolution of 18% FWHM or better for 1 MeV electrons in every cell.
The calorimeter must give a time resolution of 0.6 ns (sigma) or better at 1 MeV, to reject electrons that cross the detector from outside.
The energy of each electron of a decay is used individually: any two electrons entering a wall at points at least 40 cm apart must deposit their energy in different cells, whose energies are measured separately.
Every cell must be at least 3 cm deep so that it fully absorbs 3 MeV electrons, and every part of the calorimeter must work in the 3 mT field.

A planar tracker-calorimeter detector searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 100Mo (Q = 3.03 MeV) in an underground laboratory under 3000 m water equivalent of rock.
About 9 kg of enriched molybdenum is made into foils of 45 mg/cm2 hung in a single vertical plane, 6 m long and 3.5 m high.
On each side of the plane a tracking volume 50 cm deep, filled with Geiger-mode drift cells in a helium-based gas, reconstructs every electron track and its vertex on the foil.
A 3 mT magnetic field parallel to the foil plane fills both tracking volumes and curves the tracks so that electrons are told apart from positrons; the track curvature determines only the sign of the charge.
Each tracking volume is closed by a calorimeter wall of polystyrene scintillator cells with 19 cm x 19 cm faces and 11 cm depth, each viewed through a 30 cm acrylic light guide by a 76 mm photomultiplier sitting behind an iron plate.
The present cells give an energy resolution of 20% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of 0.30 ns (sigma) at 1 MeV.
The detector is enclosed in iron and water shielding, and the gas is flushed to keep radon out of the tracking volumes.
The calorimeter must give an energy resolution of 18% FWHM or better for 1 MeV electrons in every cell.

The energy of each electron of a decay is used individually: any two electrons entering a wall at points at least 40 cm apart must deposit their energy in different cells, whose energies are measured separately.
Every cell must be at least 3 cm deep so that it fully absorbs 3 MeV electrons, and every part of the calorimeter must work in the 3 mT field.

A planar tracker-calorimeter detector searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 100Mo (Q = 3.03 MeV) in an underground laboratory under 3000 m water equivalent of rock.
About 9 kg of enriched molybdenum is made into foils of 45 mg/cm2 hung in a single vertical plane, 6 m long and 3.5 m high.
On each side of the plane a tracking volume 50 cm deep, filled with Geiger-mode drift cells in a helium-based gas, reconstructs every electron track and its vertex on the foil.
A 3 mT magnetic field parallel to the foil plane fills both tracking volumes and curves the tracks so that electrons are told apart from positrons; the track curvature determines only the sign of the charge.
Each tracking volume is closed by a calorimeter wall of polystyrene scintillator cells with 19 cm x 19 cm faces and 11 cm depth, each viewed through a 30 cm acrylic light guide by a 76 mm photomultiplier sitting behind an iron plate.
The present cells give an energy resolution of 20% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of 0.30 ns (sigma) at 1 MeV.
The detector is enclosed in iron and water shielding, and the gas is flushed to keep radon out of the tracking volumes.
The calorimeter must give an energy resolution of 18% FWHM or better for 1 MeV electrons in every cell.
The calorimeter must give a time resolution of 0.6 ns (sigma) or better at 1 MeV, to reject electrons that cross the detector from outside.
The energy of each electron of a decay is used individually: any two electrons entering a wall at points at least 40 cm apart must deposit their energy in different cells, whose energies are measured separately.
Every cell must be at least 3 cm deep so that it fully absorbs 3 MeV electrons, and every part of the calorimeter must work in the 3 mT field.

A 3 mT magnetic field parallel to the foil plane fills both tracking volumes and curves the tracks so that electrons are told apart from positrons; the track curvature determines only the sign of the charge.
Each tracking volume is closed by a calorimeter wall of polystyrene scintillator cells with 19 cm x 19 cm faces and 11 cm depth, each viewed through a 30 cm acrylic light guide by a 76 mm photomultiplier sitting behind an iron plate.
The present cells give an energy resolution of 20% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of 0.30 ns (sigma) at 1 MeV.
The detector is enclosed in iron and water shielding, and the gas is flushed to keep radon out of the tracking volumes.
The calorimeter must give an energy resolution of 18% FWHM or better for 1 MeV electrons in every cell.

The energy of each electron of a decay is used individually: any two electrons entering a wall at points at least 40 cm apart must deposit their energy in different cells, whose energies are measured separately.
Every cell must be at least 3 cm deep so that it fully absorbs 3 MeV electrons, and every part of the calorimeter must work in the 3 mT field.

On each side of the plane a tracking volume 50 cm deep, filled with Geiger-mode drift cells in a helium-based gas, reconstructs every electron track and its vertex on the foil.
A 3 mT magnetic field parallel to the foil plane fills both tracking volumes and curves the tracks so that electrons are told apart from positrons; the track curvature determines only the sign of the charge.
Each tracking volume is closed by a calorimeter wall of polystyrene scintillator cells with 19 cm x 19 cm faces and 11 cm depth, each viewed through a 30 cm acrylic light guide by a 76 mm photomultiplier sitting behind an iron plate.
The present cells give an energy resolution of 20% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of 0.30 ns (sigma) at 1 MeV.
The detector is enclosed in iron and water shielding, and the gas is flushed to keep radon out of the tracking volumes.
The calorimeter must give an energy resolution of 18% FWHM or better for 1 MeV electrons in every cell.
The calorimeter must give a time resolution of 0.6 ns (sigma) or better at 1 MeV, to reject electrons that cross the detector from outside.
The energy of each electron of a decay is used individually: any two electrons entering a wall at points at least 15 cm apart must deposit their energy in different cells, whose energies are measured separately.
Every cell must be at least 3 cm deep so that it fully absorbs 3 MeV electrons, and every part of the calorimeter must work in the 3 mT field.

On each side of the plane a tracking volume 50 cm deep, filled with Geiger-mode drift cells in a helium-based gas, reconstructs every electron track and its vertex on the foil.
A 3 mT magnetic field parallel to the foil plane fills both tracking volumes and curves the tracks so that electrons are told apart from positrons; the track curvature determines only the sign of the charge.
Each tracking volume is closed by a calorimeter wall of polystyrene scintillator cells with 19 cm x 19 cm faces and 11 cm depth, each viewed through a 30 cm acrylic light guide by a 76 mm photomultiplier sitting behind an iron plate.
The present cells give an energy resolution of 20% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of 0.30 ns (sigma) at 1 MeV.
The detector is enclosed in iron and water shielding, and the gas is flushed to keep radon out of the tracking volumes.
The calorimeter must give an energy resolution of 18% FWHM or better for 1 MeV electrons in every cell.
The calorimeter must give a time resolution of 0.6 ns (sigma) or better at 1 MeV, to reject electrons that cross the detector from outside.
The energy of each electron of a decay is used individually: any two electrons entering a wall at points at least 15 cm apart must deposit their energy in different cells, whose energies are measured separately.
Every cell must be at least 3 cm deep so that it fully absorbs 3 MeV electrons, and every part of the calorimeter must work in the 3 mT field.

On each side of the plane a tracking volume 50 cm deep, filled with Geiger-mode drift cells in a helium-based gas, reconstructs every electron track and its vertex on the foil.
A 3 mT magnetic field parallel to the foil plane fills both tracking volumes and curves the tracks so that electrons are told apart from positrons; the track curvature determines only the sign of the charge.
Each tracking volume is closed by a calorimeter wall of polystyrene scintillator cells with 19 cm x 19 cm faces and 11 cm depth, each viewed through a 30 cm acrylic light guide by a 76 mm photomultiplier sitting behind an iron plate.
The present cells give an energy resolution of 20% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of 0.30 ns (sigma) at 1 MeV.
The detector is enclosed in iron and water shielding, and the gas is flushed to keep radon out of the tracking volumes.
The calorimeter must give an energy resolution of 18% FWHM or better for 1 MeV electrons in every cell.
The calorimeter must give a time resolution of 0.6 ns (sigma) or better at 1 MeV, to reject electrons that cross the detector from outside.
The energy of each electron of a decay is used individually: any two electrons entering a wall at points at least 15 cm apart must deposit their energy in different cells, whose energies are measured separately.
Every cell must be at least 3 cm deep so that it fully absorbs 3 MeV electrons, and every part of the calorimeter must work in the 3 mT field.

On each side of the plane a tracking volume 50 cm deep, filled with Geiger-mode drift cells in a helium-based gas, reconstructs every electron track and its vertex on the foil.
A 3 mT magnetic field parallel to the foil plane fills both tracking volumes and curves the tracks so that electrons are told apart from positrons; the track curvature determines only the sign of the charge.
Each tracking volume is closed by a calorimeter wall of polystyrene scintillator cells with 19 cm x 19 cm faces and 11 cm depth, each viewed through a 30 cm acrylic light guide by a 76 mm photomultiplier sitting behind an iron plate.
The present cells give an energy resolution of 20% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of 0.30 ns (sigma) at 1 MeV.
The detector is enclosed in iron and water shielding, and the gas is flushed to keep radon out of the tracking volumes.
The calorimeter must give an energy resolution of 18% FWHM or better for 1 MeV electrons in every cell.
The calorimeter must give a time resolution of 0.6 ns (sigma) or better at 1 MeV, to reject electrons that cross the detector from outside.
The energy of each electron of a decay is used individually: any two electrons entering a wall at points at least 15 cm apart must deposit their energy in different cells, whose energies are measured separately.
Every cell must be at least 3 cm deep so that it fully absorbs 3 MeV electrons, and every part of the calorimeter must work in the 3 mT field.

A planar tracker-calorimeter detector searches for neutrinoless double-beta decay of 100Mo (Q = 3.03 MeV) in an underground laboratory under 3000 m water equivalent of rock.
About 9 kg of enriched molybdenum is made into foils of 45 mg/cm2 hung in a single vertical plane, 6 m long and 3.5 m high.
On each side of the plane a tracking volume 50 cm deep, filled with Geiger-mode drift cells in a helium-based gas, reconstructs every electron track and its vertex on the foil.
A 3 mT magnetic field parallel to the foil plane fills both tracking volumes and curves the tracks so that electrons are told apart from positrons; the track curvature determines only the sign of the charge.
Each tracking volume is closed by a calorimeter wall of polystyrene scintillator cells with 19 cm x 19 cm faces and 11 cm depth, each viewed through a 30 cm acrylic light guide by a 76 mm photomultiplier sitting behind an iron plate.
The present cells give an energy resolution of 20% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of 0.30 ns (sigma) at 1 MeV.
The detector is enclosed in iron and water shielding, and the gas is flushed to keep radon out of the tracking volumes.
The calorimeter must give an energy resolution of 18% FWHM or better for 1 MeV electrons in every cell.
The calorimeter must give a time resolution of 0.6 ns (sigma) or better at 1 MeV, to reject electrons that cross the detector from outside.
The energy of each electron of a decay is used individually: any two electrons entering a wall at points at least 15 cm apart must deposit their energy in different cells, whose energies are measured separately.
Every cell must be at least 3 cm deep so that it fully absorbs 3 MeV electrons, and every part of the calorimeter must work in the 3 mT field.

About 9 kg of enriched molybdenum is made into foils of 45 mg/cm2 hung in a single vertical plane, 6 m long and 3.5 m high.
On each side of the plane a tracking volume 50 cm deep, filled with Geiger-mode drift cells in a helium-based gas, reconstructs every electron track and its vertex on the foil.
A 3 mT magnetic field parallel to the foil plane fills both tracking volumes and curves the tracks so that electrons are told apart from positrons; the track curvature determines only the sign of the charge.
Each tracking volume is closed by a calorimeter wall of polystyrene scintillator cells with 19 cm x 19 cm faces and 11 cm depth, each viewed through a 30 cm acrylic light guide by a 76 mm photomultiplier sitting behind an iron plate.

The detector is enclosed in iron and water shielding, and the gas is flushed to keep radon out of the tracking volumes.

The energy of each electron of a decay is used individually: any two electrons entering a wall at points at least 15 cm apart must deposit their energy in different cells, whose energies are measured separately.
Every cell must be at least 3 cm deep so that it fully absorbs 3 MeV electrons, and every part of the calorimeter must work in the 3 mT field.

The following describes a particle-physics detector.

NEMO-3 is a tracker-calorimeter double-beta-decay experiment operated in the Modane underground laboratory (LSM, Frejus road tunnel).
About 10 kg of enriched isotopes (mostly 100Mo, also 82Se, 116Cd, 130Te, 150Nd, 96Zr, 48Ca) are rolled into thin source foils arranged in a cylinder of 20 sectors.
On both sides of the foils, 6180 open drift cells operated in Geiger mode reconstruct each electron track in a 25 G solenoidal field, which separates electrons from positrons.
The tracking volume is closed by calorimeter walls of 1940 polystyrene-based plastic scintillator blocks, about 10 cm thick, each coupled, mostly through a light guide, to a low-radioactivity 3-in. or 5-in. photomultiplier.
The calorimeter reaches an energy resolution of 14-17% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of about 250 ps at 1 MeV.
Iron, water and wood shielding surround the detector, which sits under about 4800 m water equivalent of rock.
The follow-up detector will hold about 100 kg of isotope in the same tracker-calorimeter layout and aims at a half-life sensitivity near 1e26 years.
It requires an energy resolution of about 8% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons in every calorimeter cell.
It requires a time resolution of about 400 ps at 1 MeV between two cells, to reject electrons crossing the detector from outside.
Each electron of a decay must have its energy measured individually, and all calorimeter materials must keep 208Tl and 214Bi activity low enough for a 3 MeV region of interest.

The following describes a particle-physics detector.

NEMO-3 is a tracker-calorimeter double-beta-decay experiment operated in the Modane underground laboratory (LSM, Frejus road tunnel).
About 10 kg of enriched isotopes (mostly 100Mo, also 82Se, 116Cd, 130Te, 150Nd, 96Zr, 48Ca) are rolled into thin source foils arranged in a cylinder of 20 sectors.
On both sides of the foils, 6180 open drift cells operated in Geiger mode reconstruct each electron track in a 25 G solenoidal field, which separates electrons from positrons.
The tracking volume is closed by calorimeter walls of 1940 polystyrene-based plastic scintillator blocks, about 10 cm thick, each coupled, mostly through a light guide, to a low-radioactivity 3-in. or 5-in. photomultiplier.
The calorimeter reaches an energy resolution of 14-17% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of about 250 ps at 1 MeV.
Iron, water and wood shielding surround the detector, which sits under about 4800 m water equivalent of rock.
The follow-up detector will hold about 100 kg of isotope in the same tracker-calorimeter layout and aims at a half-life sensitivity near 1e26 years.
It requires an energy resolution of about 8% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons in every calorimeter cell.
It requires a time resolution of about 400 ps at 1 MeV between two cells, to reject electrons crossing the detector from outside.
Each electron of a decay must have its energy measured individually, and all calorimeter materials must keep 208Tl and 214Bi activity low enough for a 3 MeV region of interest.

On both sides of the foils, 6180 open drift cells operated in Geiger mode reconstruct each electron track in a 25 G solenoidal field, which separates electrons from positrons.
The tracking volume is closed by calorimeter walls of 1940 polystyrene-based plastic scintillator blocks, about 10 cm thick, each coupled, mostly through a light guide, to a low-radioactivity 3-in. or 5-in. photomultiplier.
The calorimeter reaches an energy resolution of 14-17% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of about 250 ps at 1 MeV.
Iron, water and wood shielding surround the detector, which sits under about 4800 m water equivalent of rock.
The follow-up detector will hold about 100 kg of isotope in the same tracker-calorimeter layout and aims at a half-life sensitivity near 1e26 years.
It requires an energy resolution of about 8% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons in every calorimeter cell.
It requires a time resolution of about 400 ps at 1 MeV between two cells, to reject electrons crossing the detector from outside.
Each electron of a decay must have its energy measured individually, and all calorimeter materials must keep 208Tl and 214Bi activity low enough for a 3 MeV region of interest.

On both sides of the foils, 6180 open drift cells operated in Geiger mode reconstruct each electron track in a 25 G solenoidal field, which separates electrons from positrons.
The tracking volume is closed by calorimeter walls of 1940 polystyrene-based plastic scintillator blocks, about 10 cm thick, each coupled, mostly through a light guide, to a low-radioactivity 3-in. or 5-in. photomultiplier.
The calorimeter reaches an energy resolution of 14-17% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of about 250 ps at 1 MeV.
Iron, water and wood shielding surround the detector, which sits under about 4800 m water equivalent of rock.
The follow-up detector will hold about 100 kg of isotope in the same tracker-calorimeter layout and aims at a half-life sensitivity near 1e26 years.
It requires an energy resolution of about 8% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons in every calorimeter cell.
It requires a time resolution of about 400 ps at 1 MeV between two cells, to reject electrons crossing the detector from outside.
Each electron of a decay must have its energy measured individually, and all calorimeter materials must keep 208Tl and 214Bi activity low enough for a 3 MeV region of interest.

NEMO-3 is a tracker-calorimeter double-beta-decay experiment operated in the Modane underground laboratory (LSM, Frejus road tunnel).
About 10 kg of enriched isotopes (mostly 100Mo, also 82Se, 116Cd, 130Te, 150Nd, 96Zr, 48Ca) are rolled into thin source foils arranged in a cylinder of 20 sectors.
On both sides of the foils, 6180 open drift cells operated in Geiger mode reconstruct each electron track in a 25 G solenoidal field, which separates electrons from positrons.
The tracking volume is closed by calorimeter walls of 1940 polystyrene-based plastic scintillator blocks, about 10 cm thick, each coupled, mostly through a light guide, to a low-radioactivity 3-in. or 5-in. photomultiplier.
The calorimeter reaches an energy resolution of 14-17% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons and a time resolution of about 250 ps at 1 MeV.
Iron, water and wood shielding surround the detector, which sits under about 4800 m water equivalent of rock.
The follow-up detector will hold about 100 kg of isotope in the same tracker-calorimeter layout and aims at a half-life sensitivity near 1e26 years.
It requires an energy resolution of about 8% FWHM for 1 MeV electrons in every calorimeter cell.
It requires a time resolution of about 400 ps at 1 MeV between two cells, to reject electrons crossing the detector from outside.
Each electron of a decay must have its energy measured individually, and all calorimeter materials must keep 208Tl and 214Bi activity low enough for a 3 MeV region of interest.
